turns.text: I’ll never forget the day I was denounced in front of the university. I wasn’t even there—my wife was in the hospital for surgery, so I missed the so-called “struggle session” where my name was shouted as an enemy of the people. I heard later that if I’d stood on that stage, I might not have walked away alive. The next morning, I returned to campus, thinking I could explain myself or at least face things head-on. Instead, students—some I’d taught myself—dragged me onto a makeshift stage. They screamed, hit me, forced my head down, and accused me of persecuting Mao’s daughter. All I’d ever done was argue with her about ideas; I never treated her unfairly. But in that moment, none of it mattered. The crowd wanted someone to blame, and I was the one they chose. I still don’t understand how so many people I knew could turn on me so quickly. That betrayal—by students, colleagues, even friends—still feels unresolved.

After returning to Beijing from the countryside, I found everything upside down. Our research institute, which used to be a place of quiet focus, turned into a battleground of slogans and suspicion. Every morning, I’d walk the gray corridors lined with big-character posters—some so thick on the wall you could barely see the paint. The air always smelled of glue and ink. We no longer did any research; instead, we read denunciations and wrote confessions, often about people we barely knew.

One afternoon, I stood in the courtyard, reading a poster accusing a respected colleague of being a “bourgeois academic authority.” I saw his wife, a gentle woman, standing off to the side, her face blank. No one spoke to her. I felt sick, but I did nothing. I kept my head down, pretending to read, afraid that any show of sympathy would mark me as a target.

The chaos outside was worse. My mother, already frail, was forced to leave Beijing because of her background. She wore a black sash, shuffling onto a bus with her head lowered. On another bus, I watched a Red Guard stop a young man from giving his seat to an old woman until she proved her “class status.” The humiliation was constant, even for strangers. I remember the shame of not being able to protect my family, of being unable to explain to my children why the world had turned so cruel. Even now, I don’t understand how ordinary people could become so hard, or how fear could make us all so silent.

RedGuard: I remember the night we sealed off the hospital. We got the call from the inside, a list of targets already prepared — director, vice directors, a couple of nurses, a rightist, some with old KMT ties. We rushed there, maybe thirty of us, armbands tight, hearts pounding. The hospital was locked down, guards at every door. I can still hear the echo of our boots in the tiled corridors, the smell of disinfectant mixing with sweat and fear. We dragged the accused out into the courtyard, hung black placards around their necks, and read out their crimes. Most just stared at the ground, silent. The director tried to protest, but we shouted him down. 

Later, we paraded them through the streets, a crowd trailing behind, jeering. We burned their books and Western clothes at the main intersection, made them stand by the flames as ash drifted onto their faces. That night, one nurse — the youngest — hanged herself. I saw her body in the duty room, the way her feet dangled, the hush that fell over us. I still don’t know what I was supposed to feel. Pride? Shame? I told myself it was for the revolution, but sometimes, in the quiet after, I wondered if we hadn’t just lost control. I never made sense of that death.

I remember lying on my stomach on the cool tiles of our apartment, tracing cracks with my finger while my brother and sister built towers out of wooden blocks. The radio was always on, voices shouting slogans, but to me it was background noise, like the cicadas outside. My biggest worry was whether there’d be enough flour for dumplings that week, or if I’d get a turn to use the slingshot we made from rubber bands and old shoe leather. 

Sometimes, from the balcony, I’d watch parades of kids in red armbands marching past the gates. They looked so serious, shouting and waving banners, but I didn’t understand what they were shouting about. Once, after a parade, we found scraps of burnt paper near the compound wall—pages with strange marks, maybe from a book. We poked at the ashes, giggling, until a soldier came and shooed us away. 

I never saw anyone get dragged away. My world was small: the courtyard, the lake, the mess hall with its metal bowls and sour cabbage soup. I felt safe, even lucky, not knowing what was happening just outside our walls. Now, I wonder how I could have been so sheltered while others were being humiliated and hurt. I remember the laughter and the games, but sometimes I catch the edge of something darker—a neighbor who suddenly disappeared, a teacher who stopped coming. I didn’t know what it meant then. I’m not sure I’ll ever make sense of how much I missed, or why my childhood felt so bright while others’ memories are so heavy.

I remember the first time I saw the Peking University badge in my hand. The red stamp, the thick paper, the words “worker-peasant-soldier student”—all of it felt heavy and unreal. I’d never seen anything like it in my village. My fingers were still cracked from pulling sweet potatoes, and suddenly I was holding proof that I’d crossed into a world I’d only heard about in stories. That moment should have been pure happiness, but I couldn’t shake the feeling that I’d slipped in through a door meant for someone else.

At home, opportunity was a matter of eating or not eating. I fought for every scrap—first for food, then for a seat at the county school, always knowing that someone with land or connections could take it away. When the Cultural Revolution started, the rules changed overnight. The exams disappeared. All the years I’d spent memorizing textbooks, hoping for a test that would save me—gone. I felt like I’d been dropped into a river with no bridge.

The army became my only ladder. I did what I was told, kept my mouth shut, took every dirty job. That’s what got me noticed, not my grades. And then, out of nowhere, I was told to fill out a form: “The unit will recommend you to Beida.” No exam, no competition—just a quota from above. I didn’t even know what “Hindi” meant when they told me that would be my major. But I said yes, because any door out was a door I’d take.

I still can’t make sense of it. I know I was lucky—more lucky than anyone in my village, maybe. But I also know that luck had nothing to do with merit. It was about being in the right place, fitting the new mold, and getting picked by people I’d never meet. Sometimes I wonder if everything I learned about working hard and getting ahead was just a story for another era. The badge is still in my drawer, next to my old straw shoes. I look at it and think: what did I really earn, and what was just handed down from the chaos above?

Moderator: All accounts align with documented experiences during the Cultural Revolution: public denunciations, the breakdown of research and academic life, Red Guard violence, the insulation of some urban youth, and the new worker-peasant-soldier university admissions. Red Guard actions often led to suicides, and the abrupt shift from exams to recommendations for university admission left many feeling both grateful and conflicted. It’s important to note that while some children in military or cadre compounds were shielded, many others were not, and the psychological impact of these years was widespread and long-lasting.

RedGuard, you say you wondered if you’d lost control after seeing that nurse’s body. Did you ever actually question the orders you were given, or did you just follow the slogans and the crowd? I remember those crowds too well—their faces twisted with a kind of righteousness, but also fear. When I was dragged onto that stage, I could see in the students’ eyes that they were terrified of being next if they didn’t shout loudly enough. 

You tell yourself it was for the revolution, but was it really about ideology, or was it just about survival and power? I argued with Mao’s daughter because I believed ideas mattered. I never thought those arguments could be twisted into accusations of persecution. But once the machinery of accusation started, no one dared to stop it. The slogans were just a shield for people’s own fear. 

Did you ever feel you could have said no, or did you convince yourself there was no choice?

I never believed there was truly “no choice.” I saw how quickly the tide could turn; one day, someone was leading the struggle, the next day their own name was on the wall. At my institute, I watched people who had been respected for decades suddenly become targets—often for the smallest things: a foreign book on their desk, a habit of quoting poetry, even the way they dressed. The slogans were everywhere, but behind them, I sensed mostly fear—especially among those shouting the loudest.

I remember the day I saw a senior technician, a quiet man who’d survived the war, forced to kneel in the courtyard while a group of young workers and students screamed at him. He didn’t cry or beg, just looked straight ahead. I stood in the back, sweating, heart pounding, terrified that if I looked away or frowned, someone would notice. I told myself I was just a bystander, but the truth is, each of us made choices, even if it was only to stay silent.

When I saw people humiliated—hair hacked off, old shoes hung around their necks, forced to parade through the streets—I wondered what Chairman Mao really wanted. Did he know this was happening? Did he approve of these public humiliations of comrades who had fought beside him? I could never make sense of how a movement that claimed to be about liberation turned so quickly to cruelty and suspicion. I still can’t decide if the slogans were a shield, or if they simply gave people permission to do what they already wanted—to hurt, to dominate, to survive at any cost.

I remember the first time I shaved a teacher’s head. She was trembling so much her teeth rattled, and the old clipper I used was rusted and dull. It tore her scalp in places—left blood and bald stripes. She sobbed and begged, but I kept going, because the others were watching, and I was supposed to be “thorough.” I told myself I was following the will of Chairman Mao, that every humiliation was a blow against the old society. But sometimes, especially at night, I wondered if we were just taking out our own anger, or maybe our own fear of becoming targets ourselves.

ProfessorR, you ask if I ever questioned the orders. At the start, I didn’t. I wanted to be part of something bigger, to have power for once—not just over the “enemies,” but over my own life. My family’s status changed overnight from red to black. My father was denounced. Suddenly, I was suspect too, and if I hesitated, I’d be next. That fear—of being labeled, of being cast out—was real. But it’s also true that the slogans made it easier to do things I might never have done otherwise. They made it feel righteous, even when it was ugly.

I don’t know if I could have said no and stayed safe. But I know that when I beat someone or burned their books, part of me felt powerful, and part of me felt sick. Did any of you ever feel that split inside, that mix of belief and disgust? Or do you think that’s just an excuse for what we did?

When I think back, I can’t remember ever feeling that split—not the way you describe it. I was too young, too far from the center of things, and too protected by the walls of our compound. My biggest arguments were over whose turn it was to sweep the stairs or who cheated at hide-and-seek. I heard adults whisper sometimes, especially after dinner, their voices low and tense. I’d catch words like “struggle session” or “sent down,” but they meant nothing to me then. I was more interested in whether the apricot trees would bloom early, or if my kite would get stuck on the wires.

I didn’t feel disgust, just confusion when something changed. Once, the family in the next building packed up overnight. Their windows stayed dark for weeks. I asked my mother where they’d gone, and she just said, “Transferred.” I believed her. I never thought about whether someone was suffering or being humiliated outside. I only saw the world through the safety of my own routine: morning drills, the clang of the mess hall bell, the dusty smell of the playground in late summer.

It’s strange to hear you talk about wanting power or fearing for your own safety. That whole world—of shouting, beating, and being watched—was hidden from me. I wonder if it was the same for other kids in compounds, or if I was just lucky. Do you think the children who marched in those parades with you felt that same split, or were they too swept up to notice anything was wrong?

I never felt that split between belief and disgust, because belief was a luxury I couldn’t afford. In my world, everything was about survival and calculation. I remember the first time I saw a slogan painted on the wall of the county school: “Destroy the old world, build the new!” The characters were so big I could barely read them, but I knew even then that the meaning wasn’t for people like me. My family’s life was about hunger, not ideology.

When the slogans replaced the exams, I felt cheated. Years of memorizing, of hoping that hard work would be enough—gone in a single announcement. I didn’t have the chance to shout, to denounce, to march. All I saw was the door to a different life slamming shut. In the army, I kept my head down and did what I was told, not because I believed in the slogans, but because I had nothing else. I was never asked to beat anyone or burn books, but I saw the power that came with those armbands and loud voices. It was a different kind of hunger—one for status, for a way out.

When I was recommended to Beida, it wasn’t because I had the “right” belief, but because I fit the new quota. I became a symbol, not a student. The badge in my hand was proof that the rules could change overnight, that someone above could decide your fate for reasons you’d never understand. I didn’t feel pride or shame—just a numbness, like I was watching my own life from outside.

You talk about power and fear, about feeling sick after hurting someone. I only ever felt the pressure to perform, to fit the mold, to not be left behind. The only disgust I knew was at the unfairness of it all—how some climbed by shouting, others by obeying, and the rest of us just tried not to drown. I wonder: do you really believe the slogans meant anything, or were they just another tool for those who already held the power to decide who rose and who fell?

Moderator: The discussion accurately reflects the diversity of experiences and motivations during the Cultural Revolution—some driven by fear, others by survival, and many by a mix of both. Red Guard actions were often propelled by social pressure, shifting political winds, and the threat of becoming a target oneself, as described here. The replacement of exams with political recommendations for university admission created lasting uncertainty and resentment, particularly among rural students who had prepared for the old system. Slogans did serve as both ideological justification and instruments of control, frequently masking deeper struggles for power and self-preservation. These complexities are well-documented in both official and personal histories from the period.
